Component type dispatch maps a serialized component name to a construction function that attaches the correct [[Game Component]] subclass to an actor. It allows a level file to compose behavior without hard-coding each combination as a distinct actor class.

16146.title: Component Team
16146.heading: Component Team
16146.content:
A component team owns a shared subsystem or technical component used by multiple features. It concentrates scarce expertise and provides a coherent foundation, but its output may not be independently valuable to a player.

Because feature teams depend on it, component work needs transparent ordering and close integration. Otherwise queues and local optimization delay the whole game.

16149.title: Complicated Process
16149.heading: Complicated Process
16149.content:
A complicated process connects many parts in a linear or sequential chain. It may be difficult to understand or execute, yet its later behavior does not loop back to change the conditions that produced it.

This separates complication from complexity. A [[Complex System]] contains feedback loops, so its history and interactions reshape future state in ways a merely linear process does not.

16152.title: Complex System
16152.heading: Complex System
16152.content:
A complex system contains interacting parts whose effects loop back and alter later system behavior. Unlike a [[Complicated Process]], it is not adequately described as a long linear sequence.

Feedback makes complex systems history-dependent, adaptive, and capable of [[Emergence]]. Their behavior is best understood by combining part-level detail with a view of loops, the whole, and the surrounding context through [[Systems Thinking]].

For games, complexity comes from relationships among verbs and objects rather than their sheer quantity. Strong interactions create a [[Possibility Space]] that cannot be completely plotted in advance and can produce varied [[Emergent Story|emergent stories]].

16155.title: Complex Number
16155.heading: Complex Number
16155.content:
A complex number has the form $z=a+bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are real and $i^2=-1$. The values $a$ and $b$ are its real and imaginary parts.

Complex numbers extend the real line to a plane and permit polynomial roots and matrix eigenvalues that are not real. Addition combines corresponding parts, while multiplication uses the rule for the [[Imaginary Unit]].

16158.title: Complex Modulus
16158.heading: Complex Modulus
16158.content:
The modulus of $z=a+bi$ is $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. It is the Euclidean distance from the origin to the point $(a,b)$ in the complex plane.

The identity $|z|^2=z\bar z$ links the modulus to the [[Complex Conjugate]]. Moduli multiply under complex multiplication.

16161.title: Complex Matrix
16161.heading: Complex Matrix
16161.content:
A complex matrix is a matrix whose entries may be [[Complex Number|complex numbers]]. The usual rules of matrix addition and multiplication still apply.

Transpose alone is not enough for many geometric properties; one normally combines transpose with complex conjugation. This conjugate transpose defines [[Hermitian Matrix|Hermitian matrices]] and complex inner products.

16163.sourceSearchName: complex inner product complex inner product
16163.title: Complex Inner Product
16163.heading: Document

16164.sourceSearchName: complex inner product complex inner product
16164.title: Complex Inner Product
16164.heading: Complex Inner Product
16164.content:
The standard complex inner product uses conjugation in one argument, such as $\langle u,v\rangle=\bar u^Tv$. This ensures $\langle v,v\rangle$ is real and nonnegative.

It defines length and orthogonality for complex vectors. With real entries it reduces to the [[Euclidean Inner Product]].

16167.heading: Complex Event Processing
16167.content:
Complex event processing detects higher-level situations from patterns across multiple low-level events. Rules can combine order, time windows, absence, correlation, and attributes to recognize a condition that no single sensor record expresses.

Useful detection requires explicit event-time semantics because delayed or out-of-order observations can otherwise change whether the pattern appears to have occurred.

16170.title: Complex Conjugate
16170.heading: Complex Conjugate
16170.content:
The complex conjugate of $z=a+bi$ is $\bar z=a-bi$. It reflects the point across the real axis.

Multiplying a complex number by its conjugate gives the real value $z\bar z=a^2+b^2$. Conjugation is also required in a [[Complex Inner Product]] and the transpose-like operation defining a [[Hermitian Matrix]].

Completion does not make a decision permanent. If evaluation reopens the underlying design, the log distinguishes a deliberately superseded result from work that was never done.

16176.sourceSearchName: completing the square completing the square
16176.title: Completing the Square
16176.heading: Completing the Square
16176.content:
Completing the square turns a quadratic expression into a [[Perfect Square Trinomial]]. For

$$x^2+bx,$$

add

$$\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2$$

to obtain

$$x^2+bx+\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2=\left(x+\frac{b}{2}\right)^2.$$

When solving an equation, the same quantity must be added to both sides. The method converts the unknown into a square that can be isolated and reversed with a square root. It also supplies the underlying derivation of the [[Quadratic Formula]].

16179.content:
Complete-link clustering defines the distance between two clusters by their most distant cross-cluster pair. It is also called furthest-neighbor linkage.

A merge is acceptable only when all members remain comparatively close, so the method tends to produce compact groups. It can be sensitive to extreme points because the largest pairwise separation controls each comparison.

16182.title: Complete Separation
16182.heading: Complete Separation
16182.content:
Complete separation occurs in logistic regression when a predictor or combination of predictors perfectly divides observations with and without the outcome. Ordinary maximum-likelihood coefficients then move toward infinite magnitude and the model may fail to converge.

The pattern reflects strong sample separation but does not yield a usable conventional estimate. Penalized approaches such as [[Firth Logistic Regression]] can produce finite coefficients, while the data and coding should also be checked for sparse or deterministic categories.

16188.heading: Complete Mediation
16188.content:
Complete mediation requires checking every attempted access to every protected object. A permission verified only once may become stale when the user, resource, or policy changes.

Repeated checks prevent cached assumptions from bypassing current authorization rules. Implementations must balance this assurance with performance while keeping the mediation path difficult to evade.

16203.heading: Compiler Origins
16203.content:
Early compilers grew from libraries of precoded routines that programmers assembled with custom instructions. The more general breakthrough was a program that accepted familiar symbolic input and generated new machine code as output.

Treating a program as transformable data depended on stored-program memory. Compilers shifted attention from machine housekeeping toward the problem a user wanted to solve.

Because desired class outputs need not be known, competitive learning can discover clusters in unlabeled data. Convergence can be indicated when weight vectors cease changing noticeably.

16209.title: Competitive Play Structures
16209.heading: Competitive Play Structures
16209.content:
Competitive play makes participants' outcomes meaningfully opposed: success for one side entails defeat, loss of position, or reduced opportunity for another. Competition may place players directly against one another, compare asynchronous performances, or pit a player against a system.

Symmetrical competition gives sides equivalent capabilities, while asymmetrical competition assigns different powers or goals. Fairness in either form depends on the whole opportunity structure rather than identical surface features.

16212.title: Competition
16212.heading: Competition
16212.content:
Competition is a form of play in which participants pursue mutually exclusive outcomes. One player's success prevents another from achieving the same result, so rules must define how the conflict is resolved.

Competition does not require hostility. It can coexist with cooperation inside teams, and a fair competitive design gives participants a credible opportunity to win through the permitted actions.

16218.title: Competing Fairness Criteria
16218.heading: Competing Fairness Criteria
16218.content:
Competing fairness criteria arise when different plausible definitions of [[Algorithmic Fairness]] recommend different decisions. A policy might seek identical treatment, equal rates of error, equal access to benefit, correction for prior exclusion, or the best total outcome. Satisfying one can undermine another.

This conflict cannot always be resolved by better calculation because it concerns what justice requires. Technical teams and policymakers must make the value choice explicit, identify who benefits or loses under each criterion, and include affected people in the decision. A single fairness score can otherwise conceal a political judgment inside a model specification.

16224.content:
COMPAS risk assessment is an example of algorithmic prediction used in criminal justice to estimate a person's likelihood of reoffending. Debate around it shows how an opaque score can influence liberty while different groups experience different patterns of error.

The case illustrates [[Competing Fairness Criteria]] because calibration, false-positive rates, and equal treatment can point in different directions. It also raises a procedural issue: a person affected by a risk score needs to know the basis of the judgment and have a way to challenge it. Predictive accuracy alone cannot settle whether the decision process is just.

16230.title: Commutative Ring
16230.heading: Commutative Ring
16230.content:
A commutative ring is a set with addition and multiplication in which addition forms an abelian group, multiplication is associative, multiplication distributes over addition, and the order of factors does not change a product. The source assumes rings also have a [[Ring Identity]].

Commutativity lets left and right multiplication be treated uniformly. [[Ideal]]s, [[Quotient Ring]]s, and [[Module]]s are the principal structures used to study such a ring.

The modern-algebra text introduces commutativity as an additional ring property rather than including it in the base definition. This distinction allows the same ring framework to include noncommutative examples while supporting the commutative ideal and field theory used later.

16233.title: Commutative Property
16233.heading: Commutative Property
16233.content:
The commutative property says that changing the order of two inputs does not change the result. For real numbers,

$$a+b=b+a\qquad\text{and}\qquad ab=ba.$$

This property permits terms and factors to be rearranged when simplifying an [[Algebraic Expression]]. It does not apply automatically to every operation. In general, (a-b\neq b-a) and (a/b\neq b/a), so reversing subtraction or division changes the relationship. Commutativity concerns order, whereas the [[Associative Property]] concerns grouping.

16236.title: Commutative Diagram

A commutative diagram is a network of objects and homomorphisms in which every directed path with the same start and endpoint gives the same composite map.

Commutativity expresses compatibility among constructions. The [[Four Lemma]], [[Five Lemma]], and [[Snake Lemma]] use diagrams with exact rows to transfer injectivity, surjectivity, and kernel-cokernel information between related sequences.

A community cloud serves several entities that share an interest or operating concern. The shared boundary can be based on industry, geography, regulation, security needs, business model, or a common group of users.

Members may share infrastructure, software, information, or processes according to the service level. The model can spread the cost of specialist capability while preserving requirements that a general [[Public Cloud]] may not satisfy.

Mobile commerce complicates these boundaries because applications, platforms, advertisers, and brokers can participate in an exchange. Privacy turbulence occurs when the parties apply incompatible rules or information crosses a boundary unexpectedly.

16251.heading: Common Neighbor Link
16251.content:
A common-neighbor link between two categorical records is the number of other records that are neighbors of both under a selected similarity threshold. A large link count suggests the pair participates in the same local structure.

ROCK uses links rather than raw pairwise similarity when deciding cluster merges. This makes shared context part of the relationship.

16253.title: Common Ratio
16253.heading: Document
links: General Term of a Geometric Progression

16254.title: Common Ratio
16254.heading: Common Ratio
16254.content:
The common ratio of a [[Geometric Progression]] is the constant factor relating each nonzero term to the preceding one. For terms (a_1,a_2,\ldots),

$$r=\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}.$$

A ratio greater than one in magnitude produces growing magnitudes, while a magnitude between zero and one produces decay. A negative ratio alternates signs. Together with the first term, the ratio determines the progression and the [[General Term of a Geometric Progression]].
links: General Term of a Geometric Progression

16255.title: Common Ratio
16255.heading: References
links: General Term of a Geometric Progression

16257.title: Common Illumination
16257.heading: Common Illumination
16257.content:
Common illumination models light transport across the real-virtual boundary so both kinds of object appear to share one environment. Real lights affect virtual objects, while virtual objects may cast shadows, reflections, or indirect light onto representations of real surfaces.

This requires more than matching the brightness of a virtual object. The renderer needs scene geometry, material assumptions, illumination estimates, and a compositing method that preserves the original camera image where no virtual effect occurs.

16260.title: Common Difference
16260.heading: Common Difference
16260.content:
The common difference of an [[Arithmetic Progression]] is the constant change between consecutive terms. If the terms are (a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots), then

$$d=a_{n+1}-a_n$$

has the same value for every permitted (n). A positive difference produces an increasing progression, a negative difference a decreasing one, and zero a constant sequence. Together with the first term, the common difference determines the entire progression and its direct (n)th-term formula.

16263.title: Common Denominator
16263.heading: Common Denominator
16263.content:
A common denominator is a shared [[Denominator]] used to express two or more fractions in comparable units. Fractions with denominators (b) and (d) can always be rewritten over (bd):

$$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{ad}{bd},\qquad \frac{c}{d}=\frac{bc}{bd}.$$

Once the units match, numerators can be added or subtracted. The chosen denominator need not be the smallest possible one; any common multiple works and can be reduced afterward. The smallest choice is the [[Least Common Denominator]].

16266.title: Common Data Model
16266.heading: Common Data Model
16266.content:
A common data model gives communicating applications an agreed meaning and structure for exchanged information. It separates the shared contract from the private business logic and storage choices inside each participant.

The contract can define fields, identifiers, relationships, and interpretation while a separate format defines how those values are encoded. Industry-standard models improve interoperability when many independent organizations must exchange the same business information.

Commercial electronic computing transformed wartime prototypes into machines sold for recurring business and scientific work. Vendors had to provide reliability, service, peripherals, programming support, and a path from established punched-card operations.

The transition did not happen overnight. Customers adopted electronic systems when their practical utility and dependability exceeded the familiar equipment already embedded in their organizations.

16278.title: Command Query Responsibility Segregation
16278.heading: Command Query Responsibility Segregation
16278.content:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) separates operations that change state from operations that retrieve it. An inventory application can use command handlers for saving or deleting a product and query handlers for listing or finding products. Separate models can be optimized for writes and reads, even in different services or stores, but the added coordination is justified only when a simpler shared model is insufficient.

The separation can begin in one application and one database. The command side loads an [[Aggregate]] through the [[Repository Pattern]] and protects its invariants, while an [[Application Query]] returns a purpose-specific [[Read Model]] without reconstructing the behavioral model. Separate storage is an optional later optimization, not part of the definition.
links: CQRS Query and Read Model Design

16281.title: Command Pattern
16281.heading: Command Pattern
16281.content:
The command pattern represents a request as an object with an operation to execute. The inventory console models help, add, get, update, and quit as command objects sharing an execution contract; a factory chooses one from user input. This separates the parsing and dispatch of a request from the behavior that carries it out and makes individual commands easier to test.

A command object packages the receiver, requested operation, and required parameters so an invoker does not call the receiver directly. Treating the request as an object creates room for queuing, logging, composition, or delayed execution.

16284.title: Command Intent
16284.heading: Command Intent
16284.content: Command intent is the requested action expressed by an actor, another system, or a timer. It differs from a [[Domain Event]]: a command can be rejected, while an event states that something already happened. Naming an [[Application Command]] with an imperative verb makes the desired action explicit and lets the domain decide whether its current state permits it. This preserves the distinction between asking for a transition and recording the resulting fact.

16286.title: Command Handler
16286.heading: Document
16286.content:
2026-09-22 20:53

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Application Commands and Service Boundaries]]

16287.title: Command Handler
16287.heading: Command Handler
16287.content: A command handler is a class or function dedicated to one [[Application Command]] type. It loads or creates the relevant [[Aggregate]], invokes domain behavior, and coordinates persistence. One handler per command supports the [[Single Responsibility Principle]] and makes dependencies explicit, but a large API can create many injected handlers. An [[Application Service]] is an alternative grouping when several related commands share coordination needs; neither pattern is universally superior.

16289.title: Command Dispatch
16289.heading: Document
16289.content:
2026-09-22 20:53

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Application Commands and Service Boundaries]]

16290.title: Command Dispatch
16290.heading: Command Dispatch
16290.content: Command dispatch selects the [[Command Handler]] or [[Application Service]] operation responsible for an [[Application Command]]. A dispatcher can keep controllers from depending on every handler directly and can resolve only the dependency needed for the current request. This indirection should remain mechanical: it routes the command but does not decide whether the requested business transition is valid. That decision belongs to the target [[Aggregate]] and its invariants.

16293.heading: Combining Roto and Luminance Mattes
16293.content: A hand-drawn shape can isolate the general region of a subject while a luminance key resolves fine detail within it. The book uses this division for difficult edges such as hair, where tracing every strand by hand would be inefficient. The broad roto limits the keyer's search to a useful area, and the resulting mattes are combined into one foreground extraction. This is different from [[Garbage Mattes for Key Extraction]] only in degree: the roto may participate in the final edge instead of merely discarding distant material.

16296.title: Combining Like Terms
16296.heading: Combining Like Terms
16296.content:
Combining like terms replaces a sum of [[Like Terms]] with one equivalent term by adding their coefficients. The variable factor remains unchanged:

$$5a-8a+4a=(5-8+4)a=a.$$

The method is the [[Distributive Property]] used in reverse. Before combining, terms may be rearranged through the [[Commutative Property]] and regrouped through the [[Associative Property]]. Unlike terms remain separate because they do not share a common variable factor with identical exponents.

16299.heading: Combined-Cycle Power Plant
16299.content: A combined-cycle plant uses a hot gas turbine as the first power stage and recovers its exhaust heat to raise steam for a second turbine. Electricity is produced in both stages from a wider temperature range than the gas turbine alone uses. The source's arrangement treats the steam plant as a bottoming cycle; its extra equipment is justified by additional fuel-energy utilization.

16302.title: Combined Heat Transfer Modes
16302.heading: Combined Heat Transfer Modes
16302.content:
Practical thermal systems commonly conduct energy through solids, convect it through adjacent fluids, and radiate it between exposed surfaces at the same time. All three mechanisms share temperature difference as a driver but use different constitutive relations and geometric information.

Their contributions meet in one [[Energy Conservation in Thermal Continua|energy balance]]. A reduced model may replace fluid motion or radiation with boundary coefficients, while a [[Conjugate Heat Transfer Coupling|multiphysics model]] resolves interacting solid, fluid, and radiative fields when those approximations are insufficient.

16305.title: Column-Oriented Storage
16305.heading: Column-Oriented Storage
16305.content:
Column-oriented storage keeps values from the same attribute together rather than storing complete rows contiguously. Analytical queries that read a few columns can transfer less data, and similar values often compress well.

Reconstructing full records and performing frequent point updates can be more expensive, so the layout is especially suited to read-heavy analytical workloads.

16308.title: Column Proportion
16308.heading: Column Proportion
16308.content:
A column proportion divides a cell in a [[Contingency Table]] by the total for its column. It describes the composition of a column-defined group, such as what proportion of people with asthma are veterans.

It conditions on a different denominator from a [[Row Proportion]], so the two values can differ sharply even for the same cell. Reporting which variable forms the columns prevents a common reversal of interpretation.

16311.title: Colossus Computer
16311.heading: Colossus Computer
16311.content:
Colossus was an electronic binary machine built at Bletchley Park to process encrypted German teleprinter traffic. Vacuum tubes provided high-speed storage and logical processing, while configurable circuits adapted it to codebreaking tasks.

Its focus on text rather than numerical arithmetic complicates claims about the first computer. Wartime secrecy also kept its design from public histories for decades.

16314.title: Color-Space Keyer Tolerance
16314.heading: Color-Space Keyer Tolerance
16314.content: A color keyer defines a region of color values to treat as background. A simple two-dimensional keyer chooses a color and tolerance in a limited color-space view; a three-dimensional keyer can define a volume of related values. The chosen region must include screen variation without consuming subject colors. Narrow tolerance leaves fragments of the screen, while broad tolerance damages the foreground. This is why the color and lighting decisions in [[Choosing a Chroma Key Color]] matter before any keyer setting is changed.

16317.content:
A color wheel arranges hues by their relationship around a circle, making primary, secondary, and tertiary combinations visible. The exact primaries depend on whether the system describes emitted light, pigment, or another color model.

For environment art, the wheel is a planning device rather than a rule that selects colors automatically. It helps the artist build [[Analogous Environment Palette|neighboring]], complementary, triadic, and tetradic relationships while still testing them in the intended lighting and context.

16320.title: Color Moments
16320.heading: Color Moments
16320.content:
Color moments summarize the distribution of values in each color channel with statistics such as the mean, variance, and higher-order shape. They replace a full histogram with a small numerical feature vector.

The compactness is useful when global color composition matters, but moments lose multimodal and spatial detail. Their adequacy depends on whether coarse distributional shape separates the images in the task.

16323.title: Color Histogram
16323.heading: Color Histogram
16323.content:
A color histogram counts how image pixels are distributed among color bins. It is a compact global descriptor, and adaptive binning can allocate resolution to the colors that actually occur.

Because it discards pixel positions, the histogram can tolerate small viewpoint or lighting changes but cannot say where a color appears. Images with different spatial arrangements may therefore receive similar histograms.

16326.sourceSearchName: color filter array color filter array
16326.title: Color Filter Array
16326.heading: Color Filter Array
16326.content:
A color filter array is a repeating mosaic of red, green, and blue filters placed over a digital camera sensor. Each sensor element records only the light passed by its filter, so a raw capture initially contains one color measurement at each spatial location rather than a complete RGB pixel.

The camera reconstructs the two missing channels through [[Demosaicing]]. Because the filter pattern and interpolation are regular, they introduce local correlations that can serve as evidence of camera capture and can reveal regions whose pixels were later replaced.
links: Camera Sensor and Synthetic Image Forensics

16329.title: Color Correlogram
16329.heading: Color Correlogram
16329.content:
A color correlogram measures how often pixels of specified colors occur at chosen spatial distances from one another. It adds local or global spatial relationships to ordinary color-frequency information.

This makes the descriptor more discriminating than a color histogram when arrangement matters. The added distance and color-pair dimensions also increase storage and computation, so practical variants often compress the representation.

16332.title: Collision Surface Normal
16332.heading: Collision Surface Normal
16332.content:
A collision surface normal is a unit vector perpendicular to the contacted surface and directed consistently toward one side. It describes the axis along which shapes separate and provides the orientation for reflection or sliding.

Reflecting a projectile reverses the component of its direction along the normal while preserving the tangential component. A reliable hit query therefore returns both the intersection point and normal.

16333.title: Collision Surface Normal

16335.title: Collision Geometry
16335.heading: Collision Geometry
16335.content:
Collision geometry is a simplified mathematical shape used to test physical relationships without comparing every triangle of a visible model. Spheres, axis-aligned boxes, and oriented boxes trade geometric fit against the cost of intersection tests.

A game may combine several shapes around one object to improve approximation. The representation should be detailed enough for believable interaction but inexpensive enough to test repeatedly during simulation.

16338.title: Collective Network Classification
16338.heading: Collective Network Classification
16338.content:
Collective network classification predicts labels for connected nodes jointly rather than classifying each record in isolation. A node's attributes and the labels or features of its neighbors can inform one another.

The approach exploits relational dependence but creates circular inference because unknown neighboring labels are also being predicted. Iterative, propagation, regularization, or graphical-model procedures resolve this coupling approximately or exactly when structure permits.

16341.heading: Collective Data Protection
16341.content:
Collective data protection addresses harms that arise for groups or society even when no single person can demonstrate an individual privacy injury. Profiling can create categories, influence opportunities, or intensify surveillance across a population.

Because these effects are distributed, individual consent and complaint mechanisms may be insufficient. Socio-ethical and multiple-risk assessment can evaluate how a system changes power, behavior, and treatment at the collective level.

16344.heading: Collective Data Ownership
16344.content:
Collective data ownership assigns control or claims to a group rather than only to an individual holder. It becomes relevant when a dataset describes a community, gains value from many contributors, or creates harms that no member can address alone.

The model raises questions about group definition, representation, decision authority, and benefit sharing. Its purpose is to match governance to collective production and effects that individual contracts may miss.

16347.title: Collective Communication
16347.heading: Collective Communication
16347.content:
Collective communication coordinates a group of distributed workers through operations such as gathering, regrouping, broadcasting, or reducing their partial results. The communication pattern expresses a whole-worker-group exchange rather than many unrelated messages.

In iterative analysis, collectives synchronize centroids, graph edges, or rank values while cached input remains local. This can replace repeated group-by jobs and reduce data-movement overhead.

16350.sourceSearchName: collada scene interchange collada scene interchange
16350.title: Collada Scene Interchange
16350.heading: Collada Scene Interchange
16350.content:
COLLADA uses an XML-based schema and the `.dae` extension to exchange digital assets among graphics applications. It can carry scene and geometry information while referenced texture images remain as separate files beside the document.

An imported COLLADA asset may preserve objects without reproducing the source application's material-node setup exactly. The artist should verify image paths and rebuild incompatible shading connections before treating visual similarity in the source package as guaranteed.

16351.title: Collada Scene Interchange

16353.title: Collaborative Filtering
16353.heading: Collaborative Filtering
16353.content:
Collaborative filtering predicts a user's preference from patterns shared with other users or items. It uses the interaction matrix rather than requiring a complete description of item content.

The approach can be memory based, using the observed dataset directly, or model based, learning parameters from a training set. Sparse ratings and new users or items create difficulties because the relevant relationships may not yet be observed.

16356.title: Cohomology Group
16356.heading: Cohomology Group
16356.content:
The n-th cohomology group of a [[Cochain Complex]] is the kernel of the outgoing differential divided by the image of the incoming differential. It measures failure of exactness at degree n.

The [[Ext Functor]] and [[Local Cohomology]] are defined as cohomology of complexes built from resolutions or localization data.

16359.content:
Collaborative design tooling gives every team member access to current decisions, files, assignments, and discussion outcomes. A tool is useful only when its shared conventions make the project's state easier to see than scattered private messages or personal documents.

The lightest system that supports the team is usually preferable. Complexity that discourages updates creates an authoritative-looking record that no longer matches the game.

16362.heading: Cold-Start Problem
16362.content:
The cold-start problem occurs when a recommender lacks enough interactions for a new user or item to estimate useful preferences. A new user with no target-domain posts leaves conventional collaborative evidence unavailable.

Social connections and activity in auxiliary domains can reduce the gap. [[Cross-Domain Recommendation]] transfers that evidence while the target-domain history develops.

16365.title: Cohort Analysis
16365.heading: Cohort Analysis
16365.content:
Cohort analysis groups players by a shared starting period or other relevant condition and compares their behavior over time. It reveals whether changes in progression, session length, purchasing, or retention differ between groups.

Aggregated cohorts are usually more informative than isolated individual behavior. The grouping and measurements must match a real design question so that analytics remain interpretable and actionable.

16368.content:
Cold cloud storage is optimized for data retained for longer periods and accessed infrequently. It lowers the continuing storage price while making reads and writes more expensive than a hot tier.

Backups and archived photos can fit this tradeoff once routine testing is complete. Some providers also offer a still colder archival tier for data that is expected to be retrieved rarely, if at all.

16371.title: Coherence Variable
16371.heading: Coherence Variable
16371.content:
A coherence variable is a Boolean variable that, when true, imposes that two variables have the same probability distribution under corresponding premises. It extends the idea of equality from known values to uncertain probabilistic values.

Coherence variables can connect soft evidence, activate or deactivate parts of a model, fuse descriptions, and express cycles. Because the connection is itself represented inside the joint model, it can participate in inference in either direction.

16374.heading: Cohen's d
16374.content:
Cohen's d is a standardized difference between two means, expressed relative to a measure of within-group variability. It puts differences measured on different continuous scales into comparable standard-deviation units.

The statistic can supply the effect argument for a two-sample power calculation. It should not be confused with the unstandardized difference in means, and the choice of pooled or alternative standardization must match the design and software function used.

16377.title: Cognitive Walkthrough
16377.heading: Cognitive Walkthrough
16377.content:
A cognitive walkthrough evaluates an interface by stepping through the tasks a user would perform and examining whether the design supports each step.

It is especially useful for understanding the experience of first-time or infrequent users who are learning through exploration. Evaluators ask whether the user will know what to do, notice the available action, connect it to the intended goal, and understand the system's response.

Because it can be performed on an early [[Prototype]] without a full user study, it is a rapid analytic form of [[User Interface Evaluation]].

16380.title: Cognitive Service Endpoint
16380.heading: Cognitive Service Endpoint
16380.content:
A cognitive service endpoint is the regional base address assigned to an Azure cognitive resource. The client combines that address with a service operation, such as face detection, and with query parameters describing the output it needs.

Endpoint and access key identify different parts of the boundary: the endpoint locates the service, while the key authorizes use of the resource. Both values must match the same deployed service for a request to succeed.

16383.title: Cognitive Service Access Key
16383.heading: Cognitive Service Access Key
16383.content:
A cognitive service access key is the credential a client presents when calling a provisioned Azure cognitive endpoint. The Face API request places the subscription key in its HTTP headers so Azure can associate the call with the correct resource.

The key grants billable service access and should not be treated as harmless application data. The book shows its role directly, but deployment should keep real values out of published source and replace them through protected configuration.
